d: A hormone-driven change of premenopausal breasts made of cysts, stromal fibrosis and apocrine metaplasia. It is bilateral, lumpy and tender before menses, and it adds no cancer risk.
A monotonous, clonal proliferation that partly fills ducts and shares some features of low-grade ductal carcinoma in situ. It raises the risk of invasive cancer about four to five times.
A biphasic tumor in which the stroma overgrows and forms leaf-like fronds. It occurs around age 50, grows fast, recurs if not fully excised, and can be malignant.
A benign papillary growth, with fibrovascular cores, in a large duct under the nipple. It is the classic cause of bloody discharge from a single duct.

Death of fat tissue, in which released fatty acids bind calcium (saponification) to form chalky deposits. In the breast it follows trauma or surgery, and foamy macrophages, multinucleated giant cells and scarring form a firm, calcified mass that mimics cancer. In acute pancreatitis, lipase digests the fat around the pancreas.
A CD30-positive, ALK-negative T-cell lymphoma that grows in the fluid or capsule around textured implants. It usually appears years after placement as a late fluid collection.
Extra nipples along the embryonic milk line from axilla to groin. It is the most common congenital breast anomaly and is often mistaken for a mole.
